purpose: Eravacycline is an antibiotic used to treat serious infections inside your belly area, called complicated intra-abdominal infections. It fights harmful bacteria that can cause these infections. It is given in a hospital or clinic setting through an IV (intravenous) line.
how_it_works: Eravacycline works by stopping bacteria from making the proteins they need to survive and grow. Think of it like jamming a machine that the bacteria depend on to function. Without being able to make these proteins, the bacteria die off and your infection gets better.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include nausea, vomiting, infusion site reactions (like pain, swelling, or irritation where the IV goes in), and low blood pressure during the infusion. Some people may also experience diarrhea or changes in liver blood tests.
warnings: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, as this medicine can harm an unborn baby and affect bone and tooth development. Avoid taking it if you are breastfeeding. It can also make your skin more sensitive to sunlight, so protect yourself from sun exposure. Like all antibiotics, it can sometimes cause a serious bowel infection called C. difficile — let your doctor know if you get severe or persistent diarrhea. Always tell your doctor about all other medications you take to avoid interactions.
typical_dosing: The usual adult dose is 1 mg per kilogram of your body weight given through an IV line over about 60 minutes, every 12 hours, for 4 to 14 days. Your doctor will decide the exact length of treatment based on how your infection responds. This medication is only given in a hospital or clinical setting by a healthcare professional.
